html:
A marble statue of Augustus as a general addressing his troops, found in 1863 at the villa of his wife Livia at Prima Porta, just north of Rome. It is now in the Vatican Museums.

It was probably carved in the early 1st century CE, perhaps as a copy of a bronze original made around 20 BCE. Augustus stands with his right arm raised, in a pose borrowed from the Greek sculptor Polykleitos's Spear Bearer. He looks forever young, though he lived to 75.

Every detail carries a message:

  • the breastplate shows a Parthian handing back the eagle standards that Crassus lost at the Battle of Carrhae, recovered by diplomacy in 20 BCE;
  • a little Cupid riding a dolphin by his leg recalls his family's claimed descent from Venus;
  • his bare feet suggest a hero or a god.

Traces of paint show it was once brightly coloured. It is one of the clearest examples of how Augustus shaped his image, and of the art of the Roman Empire as propaganda.
sum: A marble statue of Augustus as a general addressing his troops, found in 1863 at the villa of his wife Livia at Prima Porta, just north of Rome. It is now in the Vatican Museums.
